title: Roll back first
setting: A release breaks saved settings four minutes after going live.

lines.t: Nine emails in four minutes. People log in and their settings are empty.
Rolling back now. I'll look at the cause afterwards.
Don't you want to find the bug first?
Not while customers are affected. Restore service, then investigate.
How long will the roll back take?
About ten minutes. Tell people it's a known issue and we're on it.
Done. Any idea what caused it?
A migration renamed a column and the back end still asks for the old name.
The tests didn't catch that?
They used fresh accounts with no saved settings. That changes today.

title: The suspicious attachment
setting: Someone in accounts opened a file that shouldn't have been opened.

lines.t: I think I've done something bad. I opened an invoice attachment.
Is your computer still connected to the network?
Yes.
Unplug the cable now, and turn off the wifi. Don't shut it down.
Done. Some files have strange names now.
That's ransomware. The backups ran at two this morning, so we're fine.
I'm really sorry.
The email copied a real supplier exactly. You're not the first.
What happens now?
I restore from backup, and I tell everyone what to look for. No lecture.

title: Forty minutes
setting: After an outage, an engineer and her manager argue about hardware.

lines.t: The outage lasted forty minutes. Every user in Europe.
What actually broke?
The server ran out of disk at two in the morning. A reboot brought it back.
And the uptime we promise?
99.9% gives us 43 minutes a month. We spent all of it on Tuesday.
Is this the load, or the machine?
The machine. Latency had been climbing for a week before it fell over.
The board keeps asking about the cloud.
The cloud solves the hardware. It won't clear a cache nobody has looked at since March.
Then price both, the cloud and staying on-premise with new machines. Numbers, not opinions.

title: The last day of the month
setting: Support and a developer finally catch a fault that only appears on certain dates.

lines.t: Three people say the app crashes when they open two large files.
Send me the exact error message, not a description of it.
Screenshot attached. On my machine it doesn't crash, it freezes.
Those are two different things, and the difference tells me where to look.
Is it a known issue?
The bug only appears when the date is the last day of the month. We've known since June.
So why is it still here?
Because I could never reproduce the bug on demand. Today is the thirty-first.
What do you need from me?
Raise a ticket with the log file attached, and I'll debug it while the calendar is helping.

title: Never on a Friday
setting: A developer wants to release a security fix at four o'clock on a Friday.

lines.t: The patch is ready. Can I deploy at four?
On a Friday?
It worked in the staging environment.
That is the most famous sentence in this industry.
It's a security fix. It shouldn't sit until Monday.
Then it's a hotfix and we treat it like one. Who is here until eight?
Me and Rali.
Good. Roll out to 10% first, watch production for an hour, then the rest.
And if it misbehaves?
You roll back first and investigate afterwards. Write the release notes now, while you still remember what changed.

title: Your first week
setting: A senior developer explains how the team works to someone who started on Monday.

lines.t: Clone the repository and read the setup file before you write anything.
Where does the work actually happen?
The front end is what people see. The back end is where your first month will be.
What are the rules about commits?
Small ones with clear messages. Version control is how we see who changed what, and when.
Do I merge my own work?
After code review. Somebody reads it, then it goes in.
And my first task?
The integration with the payment provider. Their API returns everything in a format we convert ourselves.
Then I'll read their documentation before I write a line.

title: The weekend nobody is working
setting: Two colleagues plan a migration for the weekend.

lines.t: We migrate the old records this weekend, when nobody is working.
How much is coming across?
400,000 rows out of the legacy system that runs payroll.
The one nobody dares touch.
That one. Everything lands in the new database by Sunday evening.
Do we back up first?
We back up nightly. On Friday I'll take an extra copy and restore it somewhere safe, so we know it works.
A backup nobody has restored is a hope.
Which is why I test it. One query on the new database took twelve seconds yesterday.
Twelve seconds is eleven too many. Fix that before Saturday.

title: Two people, on purpose
setting: A manager asks what has changed since the company nearly lost its files.

lines.t: After last month, the board wants to know what we've changed.
Two-factor authentication is mandatory on every account now.
And the email that started it?
Phishing. It copied our invoice template exactly, and the malware came as invoice_final.pdf.exe.
Did anything leave the building?
No data breach. We'd have had 72 hours to report one.
Who can change things now?
Two people have admin rights, and that's on purpose. Everyone else gets permissions for what they actually do.
And the data itself?
Encryption in transit and at rest, both. The firewall handles the rest, and nobody sends credentials by email, even internally.
